The Yellowstripe scad Selaroides leptolepis, a carangid species widely distributed across the tropical Indo-Pacific, attains a maximum recorded total length of 22 centimeters [Li = 22 centimeters]. This modest body size, typical of small pelagic planktivores, is accompanied by an asymptotic adult wet weight of 124 grams [Wwi = 124 grams], a value derived from length–weight regressions for the species. Morphometric analyses of adult specimens indicate that total length at puberty, marking the onset of gonadal recrudescence, is approximately 11.9 centimeters [Lp = approximately 11.9 centimeters]. Correspondingly, the estimated wet weight at which 50 percent of individuals are reproductively mature is 20.1 grams [Wwp = 20.1 grams], a value that reflects the allometric scaling of body mass with length. These size thresholds suggest that sexual maturation occurs well before the attainment of maximum body size, a pattern consistent with an opportunistic reproductive strategy observed in many small tropical carangids.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C], embryogenesis and subsequent eclosion occur rapidly. The incubation period from fertilisation to hatching of the yolk-sac larva lasts approximately 7 days [ab = approximately 7 days], a duration that aligns with the fast developmental rates expected for pelagic eggs spawned in warm tropical waters at a temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C]. At the moment of hatching, the newly emerged prolarva possesses an initial wet weight of just 0.000523 grams [Wwb = 0.000523 grams], a mass consistent with the small egg diameter of roughly 1 millimeter. This extremely low birth mass reflects the minimal provisioning of yolk relative to adult size and imposes a brief period of endotrophic existence before the yolk-sac larva must transition to exogenous feeding, a critical bottleneck in early survival.

Maximum longevity for Selaroides leptolepis has been estimated at 5 years [am = 5 years] based on otolith increment analyses of wild-caught individuals maintained at the same experimental temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C]. This relatively short lifespan is typical of small, fast-growing carangids that experience high natural mortality rates. Mortality from predation is particularly intense during the pelagic larval and early juvenile stages, and only a small fraction of recruits survive to reach reproductive age. The trade-off between rapid growth to maturity and a compressed adult lifespan shapes the species' overall life-history strategy, prioritising early and repeated reproductive events over extended somatic persistence. Field recapture data corroborate that few individuals exceed 4 years of age in natural populations.

Reproductive output in the Yellowstripe scad is substantial, reflecting its pelagic spawning mode and the high fecundity typical of the Carangidae. Based on comparisons with the congener Caranx ignobilis, the maximum realized daily egg production is inferred by combining data on batch fecundity and spawning frequency. Females produce approximately 214 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 214 eggs per spawning event] and can spawn once per day [F_R_i = spawn once per day] during the peak reproductive season at 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C]. This high-frequency spawning, sustained over several months, generates a large cumulative annual output. The energetic demands of such continuous gamete production are met by a diet of zooplankton and small crustaceans, which are abundant in the warm, nutrient-rich surface waters of its habitat.

Comparative life-history analysis places Selaroides leptolepis among the more r-selected members of the Carangidae, characterised by small adult body size, early maturation, and high reproductive effort. The body mass at puberty, roughly 20.1 grams [Wwp = roughly 20.1 grams], represents only about 16 percent of the ultimate adult wet weight of 124 grams [Wwi = 124 grams], indicating that most somatic growth occurs after the onset of reproductive maturity. This pattern of determinate growth, where length increases decelerate markedly after puberty, is common in pelagic teleosts.
